This comment exists because people don't understand what stealth actually means. Contrary to popular myth stealth technology does not mean invisible to radar. Stealth is never used all by itself. It is used as part of a procedure and technique. Stealth provides a minimal radar return. Which means it can still be seen. The only question is at what range does it provide a significant return? To further combat this specific routes are always planned so as to minimize the return afforded by multiple radar and AA sites.

This is further confused by the fact that civilian radar systems are rather low power. Whereas military radar systems use several orders of magnitude more power. The difference is that to civilian radar they actually are invisible simply because the radar output is relatively so weak, the complimentary return is undetectable. Civilian radar actually requires active participation for aircraft; see transponders.

Additionally, stealth technology is designed to counter specific radar frequency ranges. Radar frequencies are picked because of frequency characteristics which allow for propagation and minimize attenuation. But if you have a frequency source outside of the common radar frequencies, stealth technology isn't nearly as effective. So for example, a passive radar system built on popular cell frequencies are actually somewhat effective against stealth.

What does all this mean? Well, it means that if you have an old military radar system and are close enough to the aircraft you can in fact shoot down a stealth aircraft. Especially with first gen stealth technology. That's not a failure of stealth technology but a pragmatic reality.
